title: Confusion Matrix
body:

[[Sensitivity]]
[[Specificity]]

---

The whole evaluation of a [[Binary Classification|binary classifier]], in four numbers. Rows are
what the model said, columns are what was true:

| | **Actually positive** | **Actually negative** |
|---|---|---|
| **Predicted positive** | [[True Positive]] (TP) | [[False Positive]] (FP) |
| **Predicted negative** | [[False Negative]] (FN) | [[True Negative]] (TN) |

Everything else is a ratio of these cells, and **which way you slice the table is the entire
subject**:

| Metric | Formula | Slices | Asks |
|---|---|---|---|
| [[Sensitivity]] (recall) | $\dfrac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP}+\text{FN}}$ | truth column | did you find them all? |
| [[Specificity]] | $\dfrac{\text{TN}}{\text{TN}+\text{FP}}$ | truth column | did you leave the rest alone? |
| Precision | $\dfrac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP}+\text{FP}}$ | prediction row | were your calls right? |
| Accuracy | $\dfrac{\text{TP}+\text{TN}}{\text{total}}$ | everything | **usually the wrong question** |
| F1 | $\dfrac{2 \cdot \text{P} \cdot \text{R}}{\text{P}+\text{R}}$ | both | one number when both matter |

**Down the columns is base-rate independent; across the rows is not.** [[Sensitivity]] and
[[Specificity]] are properties of the model, unchanged if you add a million easy negatives to the
test set. Precision and accuracy both move when the class balance moves, which is why they mislead
on rare positives. See [[True Negative]] for the arithmetic and [[Bayes Theorem]] for why.

Two more things the table makes visible:

- **The threshold slides you along a curve.** A classifier outputs a probability, not a label, so
  the matrix is only defined once you pick a cut-off. Lowering it moves cases from the bottom row
  to the top, buying [[Sensitivity]] with [[Specificity]]. Plotting that for every threshold at
  once is an ROC curve.
- **It generalises past two classes.** For $k$ classes it is $k \times k$, correct predictions on
  the diagonal, and the off-diagonal cells tell you *which* confusions the model makes. On
  [[MNIST]] the interesting entries are 4-versus-9 and 3-versus-8.

---

Pointer added 2026-08-16 from [[STATISTICS]], ahead of this folder's own pass: **this
table and a statistician's Type I / Type II error table are the same four cells.** A
[[False Positive]] is a Type I error at rate $\alpha$, a [[False Negative]] is a Type II error at
rate $\beta$, [[Sensitivity]] is statistical power $1-\beta$, and [[Specificity]] is $1-\alpha$.
It is also a $2 \times 2$ contingency table, so a [[Chi-Square Test]] tests it for independence.
See [[Type I and Type II Errors]] for the full translation and for why precision collapses on rare
classes.
